speechtext: I do not understand that he was making any charges against a member of the house but rather he was going back into ancient history.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not called upon to answer the hon. gentleman's question.
One of the difficulties with which this government has had to deal is foreign exchange. Owing to our heavy purchases of war materials in the United States and our domestic purchases, notwithstanding the restrictions that have been placed on the latter, the value of our dollar has depreciated considerably in the United States market. Everything must be done to prevent a further decline, and, if possible, to bolster up our dollar.
I was not in the house this afternoon when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) was speaking, and I do not know what he said. But if further restrictions are to be imposed against imports I have just this to say. I believe that the people of Canada are willing to go any length in self-denial, provided that there is equality in that self-denial and that proper safeguards are thrown out so that any interests which might be protected are not in a position to exploit the common people. More and more, as this war goes on, we see that this continent must become a vast arsenal for the British empire.
The other way in which we might improve our foreign exchange situation is by the acquisition of United States dollars through our tourist trade, and I wish to speak for a few minutes about that. Representing as I do perhaps the most popular tourist district in Ontario-and I do not think the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) or the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. McNevin), whose ridings adjoin mine on the north and east, will think I am extravagant in making that claim-I feel I can speak with some knowledge of the tourist business.
Possibly I should ask the indulgence of the house while I say something about Muskoka.

The Address-Mr. Furniss,
Muskoka is a district comprising some twenty-two townships lying about one hundred miles north of Toronto and skirting Georgian bay on the eastern shore. It is a land that was at one time covered with as fine a growth of pine timber as could be found anywhere in Canada. That forest has long since disappeared under the lumberman's axe, but a second growth of greater variety and far greater beauty has come up to take its place. From the time the foliage comes out in the spring, all through the summer, and particularly in the early autumn when the frosts have changed it overnight into a blaze of glory, with all the tints ranging from crimson to golden, it is a land of almost indescribable beauty.
Muskoka has three different lake systems on which steamers of excursion size ply back and forth carrying passengers and delivering freight and mail to different resorts along the shores. On one of these lake systems there is the most popular daily cruise anywhere in Ontario. Twelve hours' sail on smooth waters in and out among the islands, into the bays and round the headlands of three lakes, is a day's pleasure that will long remain in the memory of any tourist.
On one occasion when it was my privilege to be on one of these trips I was in conversation with several Americans and I became curious to know how many there were and where they came from. As soon as the boat landed I hurried to the parking ground and counted thirteen cars bearing United States markers, representing seven different states of the American union, two of them from such long distances as Nebraska and Florida. I mention this to show the distances from which tourists come. Speaking of this, I was at one summer resort when there was a convention of the Woman's Missionary Society and there were representatives from forty different countries including Japan and China.
We can get from our bureau of statistics or from the travel bureau some indication of the value of the tourist business to Canada, but to get a more exact idea I asked a banker who transacts most of the business for a number of United States tourists what they were spending, and he told me that one small group from Pittsburgh, comprising twenty families, spent $100,000 annually in Muskoka, or an average of $5,000 per family. Moreover, there were six groups that spent in the lower thousands and others who spent in the hundreds.
The tourist business does not benefit only those who cater to the trade; there is scarcely a person in Canada who does not benefit in some way or another. A year or so ago I listened to an address by the deputy minister
of game and fisheries of Ontario and he told us that the tourists who came to Canada every year consumed the beef from 60,000 head of cattle. That is about one-third of the quota we are allowed to send to the United States under the reduced tariff in our trade agreement with that country. Besides that, they consumed in like proportions bacon, butter, milk, eggs and all other farm produce, all of which is bound to benefit the farmer to a great extent.	.
My object in saying this is to call attention to the decline that has taken place in the tourist business in the past year. I have some figures from the travel bureau showing the number of people who entered Canada from the United States in the months from January to September, 1940 and 1939, and in every month there is a decrease except in February and March. In these months there was an increase of 69,000 in February and 82,000 in March over the same months of last year, this being due probably to the better advertising of winter sports in northern Ontario and Quebec. All other months show a decline, the heaviest being in July, when there were 1,252,173 fewer tourists from the United States than in July, 1939. That was largely due to misunderstanding about the regulations for getting in and out of Canada, but there was a decline of 17-4 per cent throughout the nine months. Some of that was on account of enemy propaganda in the United States.
What I should like to impress upon the government is that every possible means should be used to combat that propaganda. I understand that the travel bureau have in mind an intensified programme of advertising for this summer. They should begin early and continue it throughout the season. While I am speaking of that, I might mention that I had a letter just yesterday from the proprietor of one of the largest hotels in Muskoka, and he was quite sceptical about restrictions that might be placed on oranges and grapefruit and possibly lemons coming from the United States during the tourist season. He said that United States tourists were in the habit of getting these things for breakfast; that a breakfast without them was not a breakfast at all to them, and that if the first meal in the day was spoiled, the whole day was spoiled. I would urge upon the government then to do everything possible to attract tourists to the Dominion of Canada as a means of increasing our supply of United States dollars.
I am now going to refer for a few minutes to the situation of agriculture relative to the other industries of our country. I am going to quote again a few words from the speech.
The Address-Mr. Fumiss,

of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff). He said, as reported on page 474 of Hansard:
We never did get a fair deal from any government, least of all from this one. . . .
I believe I am quite safe in saying that this government has done more for agriculture than any other government that has existed since . confederation. The deal that any industry gets from a government is the way that industry is affected by the policies of the government. And in my opinion the best judges of any policy are the people.
Let us look for a moment at what has happened in the last ten years in Canada. We had an election in 1930; the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett led the Conservative party in that election, and he promised that he would make the tariffs fight for the farmer just as they fought for the industrialists. The people took him at his word and elected him to office with a substantial majority. He immediately put his high tariff policy into effect, and for the next five years the farmers of Canada suffered from the most restricted -markets and lowest prices they had ever had since confederation.
In 1935 we had another election. The present Prime Minister appealed to the country on his agricultural and other policies. The result of the election was that he was returned to office with the largest following that any prime minister in Canada ever had. He concluded trade agreements with the United States and with other nations. After five years he appealed to the country again, and on March 26 last, notwithstanding the roads being in a worse condition than at any election ever held in Canada he was returned to office, again with the largest following a Canadian prime minister ever had. That, I believe, is proof that the policies of the Liberal party are popular policies and that the farmers are not getting from this government the worst deal they ever had.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Huron North is a farmer, but he should know that the agricultural problem is an economic one, or perhaps I might say a problem of organization. The farmer is an unorganized individual living in an organized world. And the higher the degree to which industry and finance-and I include labour-are organized, the more impoverished the farmer becomes. He is like a shorn Iamb, and that is why he must have government assistance if possible.
I would not add the weight of another straw to the burden under which the government are labouring. They are working under tremendous strain. But I believe that the function of a

member of parliament is to represent his people, and if I fail to let the government know what the people at home are thinking I fail in my duty to my constituents and to the government as well.
I come now to a couple of complaints that come to me from my riding. One relates to the high wages paid on ordinary construction work, and the other to the price of bacon in the new contract. These complaints come to me in the form of letters and resolutions, and from the man on the street. The last time I was home, a couple of weeks ago, I met a man and the first words he said to me were: "You are a member of parliament; can you tell me why the government pays such high wages for ordinary construction work?" I said, "Would you complain if you were a workman?" And I reminded him at the same time that labour had had several lean years. "Well," he said, "I am a taxpayer, and I look at it from the taxpayer's viewpoint."
Some time before that I was at a ploughing match and I came across a group of farmers who were in earnest conversation. I knew some of them and joined the group, and the same question was put to me. They said that men were quitting work on the farm, going where they could earn these high wages, and it was creating a serious labour problem. One man said that they expected to be asked even $70 a month for next summer. Put it at $50 a month, which was the highest wage paid during the last war, when farm produce was double the price it is to-day, and add to that $20 for board, for which the farmer should have credit, and you have still $70 a month. Multiply that by seven or eight for the months of hire, and you have about $500. Divide that by what the farmer will get at the prices at which bacon or hogs are going to sell under the new contract, and you will find that it will take between thirty and thirty-three hogs to pay a man's wages for the summer. If you follow that through, you will find that at the average consumption of grain per one hundred pounds of live hog, it will take six to seven hundred bushels of grain to feed those hogs. I have no objection to good wages being paid if the farmer is in a position to pay them. But there will be few men hired next summer on the farm if wages are at that rate.
I have no fault to find with the price of bacon that the Minister of Agriculture got from the British government. I believe he made the best bargain possible. We must remember that Great Britain is sore pressed. All that stands between us and Hitler is the British navy. Britain's soldiers and sailors

The Address-Mr. Bourget
are in the far east, on the Mediterranean, on the Atlantic, and perhaps at many other places that we know nothing about. Britain's financial resources are not inexhaustible. The time may come before this war is over, when we may have to make common cause with Great Britain and help to feed her soldiers and sailors as we are feeding our own. If that time comes, I know that Canada can and will respond. But if industry and finance can enjoy profits and people can enjoy large salaries, then something should be done to see that the farmer gets his just share of the national income. Next summer the farmer and his wife and family will be working harder and for longer hours than any other class of people in Canada. Again I say that he should get a just return for his labour.
There are two ways by which that might be done. The first would be for the government to exercise more of the powers that have been conferred upon it by the National Resources Mobilization Act. That would be a drastic step and I know it would end in the dislocation of industry and the slowing up of our war work. But I cannot conceive of victory coming out of a struggle such as this if the only incentive to battle is monetary gain, whether it be through profits, high salaries or high wages. That should not be the yardstick with which to measure our war effort. Only when every able-bodied man in Canada is either in the army, the navy or the air force, or at work in the factory or the field producing the essentials of war, will it be possible to say that our war effort is at its maximum. It may be that before this war is over, we shall be fortunate if we are well fed, well clothed and comfortably housed, and beyond that looking for nothing but victory. The other step that I might suggest would be further taxation on profits and incomes to reduce the inequality, and the money gained thereby might be used to reimburse agriculture in some measure.
In the meantime the message I would give the farmer, if by any chance it should reach his ears, is that he should carry on. Remember, we are receiving twice as much as we received for our products during the lean years from 1930 to 1935. Even if nothing *can be done I would still say, carry on until victory is achieved, and when that time *comes we can set about the construction of a more just and equitable order.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read just a few lines from the Magazine Digest for November, 1940. This afternoon I heard the Prime Minister state that the Germans did not understand our mentality.
I quite agree that this is the situation with most Germans, but these are the words of one German who does understand it:
The British nation will be considered the most valuable ally in the world as long as it can be counted upon to show that brutality and tenacity in its government, as well as in the spirit of the broad masses, which enables it to carry through to victory any struggle that it once enters upon, no matter how long such a struggle may last or however great the sacrifice that may be necessary or whatever the means that have to be employed; and all this even though the actual military equipment at hand may be utterly inadequate when compared with that of other nations.
There is just one word in that paragraph that I do not like; that is the word "brutality", but when I tell you, sir, the name of the author of that statement, you will not be surprised at that word being included. At the end of this short article it states that these words were written by Adolf Hitler, and appeared in the original edition of "Mein Kampf". Leaving out the word "brutality", I do not think it would be possible to give a better description of the spirit of the British people; and I do not think we in Canada could do better than to foster and emulate that spirit. It is the spirit that won over the Spanish armada, that won through at Camper-down, at Trafalgar, at the Nile and at the battle of Waterloo; it is the spirit that will win out in this struggle. England has been born again in a welter of sweat and blood. England will live on. There will always be an England.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising as I do for the first
time in this house, I may be permitted, at the outset, to fulfil a most pleasant duty, in tendering my heartfelt thanks to the men and women of my constituency who have done me the honour of electing me as their representative in the nation's parliament. To the best of my modest ability, I hope to become worthy of their confidence by performing my duties with the utmost sincerity and energy.
I also wish to tender my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Claxton) and seconder (Mr. Jutras) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for having performed so splendidly on that occasion.
I fully realize, Mr. Speaker, the heavy responsibilities that are mine in these troublous times. In my constituency, at the last election, the electors-and especially the older ones- have recognized the necessity of electing a young representative because, to their mind, it will devolve upon the younger generation to rebuild what is now being laid in ruins and, especially, to find a way of solving the serious problems that will arise after the war.
The Address-Mr. Bourget

As a representative of that younger generation in this house, I wish to make a few remarks upon a matter of special concern to the younger Canadians, and one which affects directly our war effort. During this session and even during the last one, quite a few members of this house have brought that matter to the attention of the government. I know that many others, and among them my good friend and colleague the hon. member for Quebec West and South (Mr. Parent) never lose an opportunity to draw it to the attention of the proper authorities. The question I refer to, Mr. Speaker, is the technical training of the youth of Canada. We have heard it stated on all sides that this country's war effort would consist in supplying the empire and our allies with their requirements in foodstuffs and munitions.
Only a few days ago the newspapers carried a statement of Mr. Arthur Greenwood, minister without portfolio in the British war cabinet, to the effect that Canada had been transformed into an industrial country. He added that the supplies provided by Canada had been precious in quality and in quantity. He stated further that North America would soon become an arsenal. I believe all hon. members have likewise read the statement of the British minister of shipping that England was now losing more ships than she could replace. This is probably what led the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) to declare that we should have to prepare ourselves to build destroyers and cruisers in Canada. Then, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) informed us in his able review of the activities of his department that $255,000,000 would be appropriated for the establishment of new war industries.
The necessity and urgency of these industries necessarily brings up the problem of providing skilled workmen. If a lack of skilled labour is already felt, what will it be when all these new industries have been established? It is all very well to have numerous industrial establishments, but they are entirely useless without the trained labour required to operate them. The training of this labour is a question to be considered by the government.
At the risk of being charged with provincialism, Mr. Speaker, I shall very briefly call the government's attention to the situation at present existing in the province of Quebec. That province now has five or six technical schools and a few other establishments called arts and craft schools. According to the information I have been able to gather, these schools cannot fulfill the growing

demand on the part of young men eager to follow their courses. Recalling the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply that $255,000,000 were to be spent on the creation of new war industries, I wonder if it would not be good policy, especially in the present extraordinary circumstances, to devote part of this money to the construction and equipment of new technical schools. In addition to providing trained labour for our war effort, the government would thus render a valuable social service in providing the youth of Canada with a technical training which they could use to advantage later on.
I particularly wish to call the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty), who is the minister responsible for the administration of the youth training plan, to a question which I have specially at heart, as it directly interests the people of my constituency. In Levis county there are two shipyards where corvettes and mine-sweepers are now being built. According to the statement of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs, they will probably be called upon before long and for many years to come to build destroyers and cruisers. You will readily agree, Mr. Speaker, that the men who are working without respite on the construction of these ships, putting in days of twelve, fourteen and even sixteen hours, cannot continue doing that without endangering their health. In this regard, I wish to congratulate labour in general on their splendid energy and patriotism in working night and day to help achieve the victory which we all so ardently hope for. It will therefore be necessary, perhaps sooner than we expect, to replace these workmen or at least provide them with help in the accomplishment of their arduous task.
If I may be permitted to do so, I should like to offer to the responsible minister a suggestion which I consider applicable to shipbuilding as well as to many other war industries. As the minister said on Thursday last, it is absolutely necessary to provide a supply of skilled labour and to do so quickly. In accordance with the youth training plan, an agreement would first have to be made with those industries that have been given war contracts, so that such industries may employ one young workman for every five or six skilled workers. The selection of these young candidates would be made through a board of examiners that might include one repre-

The Address-Mr. Bourget
sentative from the Department of Labour, one from the company or industry concerned, and one skilled workman having some general knowledge of such industry. Mr. Speaker, I fully realize that it would not be advisable to employ all applicants without first ascertaining that they have the requisite intelligence and the necessary fitness for some particular trade. The selection of candidates having been made, the latter might begin to work in the industry concerned in order to gain some practical knowledge, but they should at the same time be required to sign an agreement to attend, two or three evenings a week, a technical school giving theoretical courses directly connected with the occupation assigned to them. After a period to be determined by the authorities, these young apprentices would have to pass an examination so as to prove conclusively that they have the necessary qualifications to hold their positions and be recognized by the examiners as skilled workers in their respective trades. I sincerely believe that if this suggestion were adopted we would have no trouble to find in a very short time all the skilled labour required by our industries. Naturally, these young men should receive during their training a minimum salary which would cover their living expenses, and in certain deserving cases would allow them to contribute to the upkeep of their dependent relatives. I have often met, especially after my election as a member of this house, parents who claim that they cannot afford to pay the expenses incidental to such training, such as transportation, clothing and the like. Payment of such salaries could be shared equally by the federal and provincial governments and by the firm or industry concerned.
I am convinced that there would be objection on the part of the companies. If they objected, the governments could easily overcome the difficulty through a clause in the contracts which would force the companies to contribute their share. I can assure the minister of labour that he would have the willing cooperation of our provincial government, because our newly elected provincial secretary declared recently that the question of technical education in our province would receive the best consideration from the government. I hope that there will be no delay and that thanks to the help of the central government our young people will soon be given the opportunity of enlarging their field of knowledge and of preparing themselves for the struggles of life.
In these few observations, I have given but a very incomplete summary of this most important question which I wanted to bring
to the attention of the hon. members of this house. Moreover, if my suggestion were adopted, we would not only further the training of our youth, but we would also make an important contribution to our war effort. I hope that it will receive the best consideration.
I also wish to call the attention of the government to a question that has already been brought up in this house, that of the salaries paid to the clerks and stenographers grade 1 in the civil service. In my opinion the salary paid to those employees is ridiculous, and so is the difference of S30 between the minimums of grade 1 and grade 2. It seems to me that a minimum of $75 would only be fair, and it is hard to understand how they can live on a salary of $60 per month from which taxes are deducted.
(Text) Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words with regard to our war effort. Since the opening of this session we have heard it stated many times that the government should have displayed more activity in the prosecution of Canada's war effort. I think every fair-minded citizen will agree with me when I say that our government has put forth a supreme effort to help our allies by supplying them with men and materials. This fact has often been stated and restated by British officials.
Before concluding my remarks, may I say that I consider it a privilege and an honour to extend my sincere appreciation to the English-speaking members in this house who have paid such fine tribute to the Freneh-Canadians. I can assure them that their heartfelt expressions will long be remembered by my fellow citizens. These members have done more for unity than the unjustified statement which can be read on page 409 of Hansard. I quote:
There is just one other mystery upon which I should like to comment. Who will stand in his place in this house and say that to-day our front line trenches are not on the English channel and along the shores of the Mediterranean? No one even thinks otherwise, but I want to recall a statement that was made in this house not so very long ago, in which we ivere told that the Canadian parliament would decide to what extent, if any, Canada would participate in this war. I think all lion, members will recall that statement. Then if we turn to page 225 of Hansard for this session we find a question which was asked and answered; hon. members can look it up for themselves. And the minister hastened-yes, hastened-in reply to the question asked, to assure some unseen minority, a handful of men, wherever they may be in Canada, men who were once described as those who wanted to run to the bush in the event of an emergency, that notwithstanding anything connected with the extension of the training period they would not have to serve outside of Canada. I have no thought but to condemn anybody who does
The Address-Mr. Bourget

not recognize that our front line of trenches is on the English channel and in the Mediterranean. I have no apologies to offer when I make that statement.

Who made that
statement?

speechtext:
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart). I do not think that represents the opinion of all English-speaking Canadians. If it did, we could not even dream of unity, here in Canada. Similar statements were made during the last war and they resulted in creating disunion and in turning Canadian against Canadian. In times like these when unity is so important, we should refrain from making such statements. It is unnecessary to recall the part which was taken in the building of our beloved country by this unseen minority. This has been proven again and again by others than French-Canadians.
I may assure you, Mr. Speaker, that French Canada is doing its utmost to help the government in the prosecution of its war effort. It may be that the people of that part of Canada have different ideas as to the means to be taken to carry on this war effort, and I think we must admit that this attitude cannot be totally condemned. For example, I think the declaration to-day of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) touching upon conscription goes to show that it is often better to base criticism on the long-range view rather than upon the narrow perspective of the moment. I am sure that no true Canadian will for one minute doubt the loyalty and sincerity of the French-Canadian. When the gods of war shall decree again, as they necessarily must, that the sun of victory will again cast its rays of peace upon the whole British empire, it will then be found that every Canadian from Halifax to Vancouver will proudly and justly maintain that he did his bit to carry on to the successful end.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking advantage
of the first opportunity to congratulate the mover (Mr. Claxton) and the seconder (Mr. Jutras) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
During the few minutes at my disposal I intend to bring to the attention of the house a matter which I think might well be given consideration at this time. This is something which I believe is important in view of the serious situation which is facing us at the moment. I refer to the menace which has resulted from the empire's shipping losses. There seems to be no doubt that this situation has reached serious proportions.

We saw in the last war what a menace this might be. A few days ago the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) related how the building of ships in his department had increased to 155, and he said that before the end of the next fiscal year that number would be increased by another one hundred. I want to congratulate the minister in that regard. But while we are making great strides in our naval shipbuilding programme, there still remains the question of our merchant marine, the question of making up the losses or, shall I say, of helping Britain to make up the losses in merchant shipping that she is suffering at the present time. I believe the time has come when we should have not only a naval shipbuilding programme but a shipbuilding programme for our merchant marine in such proportions that in some measure at least its effect would be felt in this day of world shipping losses.
I said that we are facing a menace in empire shipping. The Prime Minister of Great Britain, speaking in the British House of Commons on November 5, about three weeks ago, said in part:
The dangers in the air are sudden, but the dangers to our sea-borne traffic mature much more slowly, but they are none the less formidable and if in any way neglected they would touch the life of state. We must expect that next year still heavier U-boat attacks will be made upon us, and we are making immense preparations of all kinds to meet them.
He went on, and this is what I want particularly to draw to the attention of hon. members:
More serious than the air-raiding has been the recent recrudescence of U-boat sinking in the Atlantic approaches to our island.
That was three weeks ago. Last week Mr. Arthur Greenwood, minister without portfolio in the British government, apparently speaking on behalf of that government, said in a debate in the British House of Commons, I think last Wednesday :
It is true that we have suffered very heavily.
It is true that this is much like April, 1917, but though far worse than it should be, the situation is not as bad as it might have been, but for an actual increase in merchant tonnage built here. We have not quite lived up to our shipbuilding programme, but we are not very far from it and that has made an enormous difference. The shipping we have captured and the shipping transferred to us have gone into the pool; and although our tonnage now is slightly below what it was when the war started, the net loss is not considerable.
He promised that everything would be done to increase home production. He admitted further that the home production of ships was not adequate. He said that Britain

The Address-Mr. Pottier
hoped for an increased tonnage from the United States. He outlined the programme of Britain, which was made some time ago when it was planned to produce a gross tonnage of 1,300,000 tons a year. Mr. Greenwood said that they had not been able to reach that production, and he went on to say:
It would be folly to deny that the bombing assaults of recent weeks had damaged essential production in Great Britain.
In other words, not only in the past had Britain been behind, in their production but they were getting to the stage where they could not maintain even that, shall I say, backward rate of production. The shipping losses in the last two weeks have averaged some 50,000 tons a week. Taking the figures given as approximate, that Great Britain was producing some 25,000 gross tons a week, we find that she is going backward at the present time to the amount of some two million tons of shipping a year. But even these figures do not show the situation in its true light, because in addition to that loss in tonnage the shipping hauls are becoming longer. Ships used formerly to go to Norway, to the continent, and others would use the Mediterranean route; but now all that is changed and ships have to make longer hauls, so that not only is Britain going behind at the rate of two million tons of shipping a year but the freight hauls are becoming longer. That is the situation as we find it to-day.
But some members may say that we have acquired from seven to eight million tons of shipping from Norway, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Greece. But the British losses cannot be made up simply by transferring to a pool the continuing traffic supplied by ships from other countries. Moreover, this process of freighters from other countries coming into the pool has practically come to an end. It is not a recurring gain. It is not continuous like a building programme and it does not make up for the losses. That to-day is the all-important question.
Mr. Greenwood, as I said, hinted that Britain had to look elsewhere to make up this deficit, and he referred to the United States. Anyone who gives this matter a moment's thought knows that there are only two places where we can get more tonnage. It has to come, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, from other parts of the empire or from the United States.
Let me go over for a moment just what can be expected from the United States, and then, if I have time, I shall deal briefly with what we could produce in Canada in the way of wooden ships.
Mr. Hore-Belisha in the debate in the British House of Commons said that Britain can expect only about 300,000 tons of shipping from the United States. I think that was an underestimate; I think it was not reasonable. We can with profit look back to the last war to see just what amount of new tonnage was produced at that time. That is the only guide we have.
In 1917-and remember that the United States came into the war in that year-the United States produced 800,000 tons of new shipping, and in 1918, 2,600,000 tons; in 1919 they produced an all-high of 3,300,000 tons. One must remember that in 1918 and 1919 the United States had been in the war for a certain period and had got into their war stride. They were all-out with regard to their shipbuilding programme.
I do not think we can expect such a production at this time. I think we should rather take their tonnage as approximating the 1917 figure, and in 1917 the United States was in the war for about half a year. Their shipping production increased from 1916 to 1917, and in 1917 they produced 800.000 gross tons. Let us raise that up to 1,000,000 tons, for the sake of argument, and even then we shall still be 1,000,000 gross tons short of making up the annual losses in shipping. Therefore, if we take the United States estimate of production at 1,000,000 tons, it leaves other parts of the British empire the duty to do what they can to repair the sustained losses, to counteract the subtractions that are taking place from time to time. I think the time has come when Canada can well go over its own shipyards to see what its possibilities are and in what way it can help to meet the situation.
Let us see what happened in the last war so far as Canadian shipyards were concerned -because that is the only measure we have to go by. I will give the values in dollars in order to give the house an idea of the expansion that took place in shipbuilding at that time. In 1915 there was a total production in Canadian shipbuilding of $7,000,000. By 1917 this had risen to $35,000,000; in 1918 it was $74,000,000, and in 1919 it was $86,000,000. That represents the possibilities of expansion in Canadian shipbuilding, taking the years from 1915 to 1919.
Perhaps at this time it might be well for us to look over our own shipyards to see exactly what can be done with regard to ships. In 1918 we built 428 vessels with a gross tonnage of 235.000 tons and about the same amount in 1919, besides repairs. At that time we built for the imperial muni-
The Address-Mr. Pettier

tions board, forty-one steam merchantships, having a total of 132,000 tons, and forty-six wooden ships having a total of 90,000 tons.
Someone will perhaps ask what the policy of the government was in the last war. What did they do then? That might be a guide to what we should do now. At that time they were faced with the same menace; submarines were threatening British shipping, and the question necessarily came before this house. It came before the house first on May 11, 1917, when it was brought up by the Hon. E. M. Macdonald, member for Pictou at that time, and again on April 4, 1918, it was discussed. The question was then, as it is now:	Should we as a government go into a shipbuilding programme and build steel ships or wooden ships or both? Let me read from Hansard to show the policy of the government of that day with regard to this matter. I read from page 346 of Hansard of 1918 where the statement of the then Minister of Marine is reported:
I brought the matter to their attention, that the time was opportune for Canada to embark upon the building of steel ships as a national, permanent policy.
Some hon. Members: Hear, hear.
Mr. Ballantyne: And, after giving the matter very careful consideration for some months, and working out a comprehensive programme on good, sound, business lines, I brought the proposal before my colleagues in the government, and I am very pleased to state that it was unanimously decided that after the imperial munitions board contracts were completed all the berths in all the shipyards of Canada which are building steel ships would be utilized to the full in building steel vessels for the Canadian government.
That was in regard to steel ships. What about wooden ships? The policy with regard to wooden ships was stated by the same minister, as reported at page 349:
The hon. member for Maisonneuve said something about neutral ships. The Canadian government, of course, are confining their efforts entirely to ships of Canadian registry. We intend to keep our yards busy with Canadian registered ships only-ships for the Canadian government.
A large number of wooden ships have been built by the imperial munitions board for the imperial authorities, but it is not the intention of the Canadian government to have any wooden ships built. I am not prepared to express any opinion for or against wooden ships, except that with the money available for ship building in Canada at the present time, it seemed to the government the wisest policy to invest that money in steel ships only. The wooden shipbuilding yards in different parts of Canada have many opportunities at the present time for building -wooden ships. While they cannot build wooden ships under Canadian registry, they have every opportunity of building wooden ships for our allies and for neutral countries,

and some of these yards are now working on very large orders for wooden ships for allied and neutral countries.
That was the policy in. 1917; that is what happened at that time. They built steel ships only, and as a matter of fact, from that policy developed the famous Canadian merchant marine. In 1919, 1920 and 1921, sixty-three steel merchantships were built.
With that record behind us, I think we can profitably consider at this time what we should do in dealing with one phase of shipbuilding, namely, wooden ships. I am not going to deal with steel ships. Perhaps, before discussing this question further, I should congratulate the government upon the recent appointment of a controller of ship construction and repairs, with wide powers to allocate work and distribute men and machinery. The person named is well qualified, and he comes to his position with experience and ability.
At the present time, in yards for the construction of wooden ships in Canada we have about 5,000 tons of shipbuilding going on, and this, by the way, on the part of private owners, except for such wooden ships as are connected with our naval programme. In my remarks I am discussing merchantships. We have existing facilities for approximately 60,000 gross tons, for the construction of wooden ships. We are using less than ten per cent of our wooden shipbuilding capacity.
As we know, there has been discussed a programme in connection with wooden ships for Britain, and nothing that I shall say must be taken as proposing in any way to interfere with that programme. As I understand, there is nothing definite. There are no wooden ships contracted for and the matter is in an unsettled state. The opinion I urge at all times is that Britain should be given the right of way, and I do not wish my remarks to be construed in any way as interfering with that procedure. The right of way should be given to the old country for whatever ships it requires.
What I am afraid of is that Britain may not decide to build wooden ships, or may decide to build a limited number, and that we shall go back to the policy of 1917 of no wooden ships. We shall be not merely in the same position as at that time but in an immensely worse position, because then we had allies and neutrals for whom we were building wooden ships, as mentioned by the then Minister of Marine. That is what causes me to rise here to-night to make these remarks.
I should be very sorry to see a situation in which we were using perhaps ten per cent of our facilities for wooden shipbuilding,

The Address-Mr. Gauthier
while at the same time British losses were such that her shipping was going behind at the rate of two million gross tons a year. In my opinion our present facilities should be increased perhaps threefold; we could produce 150 thousand tons of wooden ships a year.
I make this reservation, that whether or not that can be accomplished depends on the importance assigned to wooden shipbuilding in relation to other industries. We have only a limited number of skilled workers in this country; if they are used in the steel shipbuilding industry, the aircraft industry, the munitions industry or any other industry, and if these industries are placed before the wooden shipbuilding industry, then that is going to restrict the production of wooden ships. But if we want to restore the wooden shipbuilding industry as one of the first into which skilled labour should be allowed to go, then we can produce in this country 150,000 tons a year of wooden ships. That is a very important contribution to the empire.
To-day ships have to be replaced at the rate of two million tons a year. With the United States producing one million tons there are still another million tons to come from somewhere, and that somewhere must be Canada and other parts of the empire. The wooden shipbuilding industry in Canada could produce 150,000 tons of that quantity. That is an important factor which must be considered.
I know and I should be frank in telling hon. members that there are some arguments against wooden ships. We who come from constituencies by the sea hear them and have to meet them, and in order that I may give the whole picture let me state those that we hear most often.
They tell us that wooden ships are of limited capacity; that is to say, a wooden cargo ship of 1,000 tons is considered a large wooden ship. They also tell us that wooden ships are limited as to speed; also that the personnel is an important factor, because if we have one ship of 1,000 tons and another of 10,000 tons, the latter like the former requires only one captain. They say, therefore, that we should go in for the larger ships because our personnel is restricted in numbers.
To meet those arguments one by one: as to the fact that the tonnage is limited, I would point out that wooden ships cost less. With regard to speed, we can produce proper models which, with the diesel engines of to-day, will maintain convoy speed, which, after all, is all that has to be considered at this time. As to personnel, I have great difficulty in convincing myself that there is much in that argument. I cannot see ships tied up at the
wharves, particularly on the Atlantic coast, because men to take them out are lacking. We have too much of the old seafaring blood in our veins, of the days of wooden ships and iron men. Such a challenge would never fail to be accepted on either the Atlantic or the Pacific coast. We come of a breed of men whose ancestors came here over stormy seas and who have lived by the sea, and when the time comes that we cannot find the men to man our ships the empire will be no more. Therefore I say that argument of lack of personnel is not one to be given any consideration.
We have gone through wooden shipbuilding eras in Canada. It is interesting to note that away back in the eighties we had 1,300,000 tons of wooden ships, over seven thousand vessels, built in the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec. With such a background as I have tried to outline, with the present rate of shipping losses and with the possibilities in regard to wooden shipbuilding that are ours, and with the importance of keeping that life-line of the empire between this country and Britain in being, it means nothing but ships, more ships and still more ships. We must realize that if the time ever comes that this line of ships crossing the north Atlantic is cut off, it means that the empire as we see it is no more. These ships passing back and forth are the pulse of our national war effort. They carry to Britain that which sustains her life and enables her to carry on her war effort. In our wooden shipbuilding industry we have an asset which can help to maintain that life-line. We have a great tradition of shipbuilding; we have the men to man them, the sons of captains who navigated them over the seven seas and made Canadian shipping familiar in every port in the world.
In view of these factors, I suggest that the government consider seriously a wooden shipbuilding programme. I realize, as every hon. member must, that these industries have to be placed in their relative importance. But I assure them that if the time comes that wooden ships are needed, every creek or cove on the Atlantic coast particularly is a potential shipyard. Shipyards will mushroom up over night-they increased from 40 in 1914 to 250 in 1918. That situation can be renewed, and I ask the government to give consideration to making use of that great national facility.

Mr. Speaker, having followed with deep attention and without prejudice the various speeches delivered during -the debate now drawing to a close, I have been able to appreciate, as many others have, the advan-
The Address-Mr. Gauthier

extent the ups and downs of one or the other belligerent will affect their holdings in war industries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What does one human life more or less matter to them, providing their pile increases! The sad part of it is that some of these men manage to acquire a reputation for great patriotism.
Such men are to be found in all countries- in the dictatorships as well as in the democracies. They have made of war a permanent industry. After the massacre of 1914-1918 they rested a little, while disposing from time to time of the products their industries continued to manufacture; we have had the Gran Chaco, the Chinese war, still going on, the Spanish civil war, and after a respite of twenty-five years, a new world war.
An author once wrote:
The masses are good-natured; they are not curious. When they find that they have been tricked _ they get angry and want to break everything. A moment later they have forgotten everything and the comedy starts again at their expense.
Should this definition be correct and the people some day cease being good-natured, what would happen?
A country's war effort can be disastrous when one forgets that nations as well as individuals can develop a form of anaemia which renders them incapable of intellectual or manual work. This anaemia declares itself when people are called upon to perform too much work for the food and care they receive. Therefore, in addition to the war effort there should be a conservation effort. Measures should be taken on a permanent basis in view of the years which will follow this effort, when the world will stop for a while to draw breath-those who will still be strong enough to do so-and to repair the losses, if the required materials still exist and especially if there is still in the world sufficient courage to undertake a proper reconstruction.
The Canadian effort, already considerable, will become even greater by force of circumstances. It should continue to be above all rational. Since our allies are asking especially for an industrial effort, it is because that is what they need-what they need more than they need men. I do not think I am wrong in stating that the people of the entire country are willing to give to Great Britain every assistance possible in the way of munitions and instruments of war. Thousands of our young men are already on active service overseas. Those who have remained here have shown their willingness to do all in, their power to ensure the defence of the country.

I shall not discuss, Mr. Speaker, the opinion of those who believe that our boundary line is in Europe. I shall simply tell them that as a citizen entitled to his own views I do not share theirs.
We need men for our industries; we have them here, let us use them. We need men to defend the fairest of the lands belonging to the free association of the countries of the empire; we have them, and I am sure they will know how to behave should Canada be attacked. The other day I heard the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) reply to the question of a fellow-member who asked him whether he was opposed to imperialism. This was the hon. member's answer:
I am opposed to that imperialism which places the empire above Canada. I am for Canada first; I place Canada above all, Canada should play her part in the empire, but we should not lose sight of the interests of Canada.
These words of the hon. member for Bellechasse awakened in me a world of recollections. I thought I was hearing the voice of one of those who were called, scarcely two or three years ago, the group of ten or the dissentients. A good idea always finds supporters in the end.

speechtext:
I do not wish to discuss the hon. member's present or past views and I take the liberty of telling him that I do not intend to labour the point.
If I might be permitted, I would ask the government to pay no heed to the out and

The Address-Mr. Gauthier
out advocates of conscription. On March 26 last, the people gave a clear cut decision on that question. From the lowliest as well as the wealthiest Canadian citizens comes this unanimous plea: carry out the mandate we have entrusted to you; we are confident that you will fulfil your task unflinchingly.
Forgetting for a moment their great financial problems to indulge, as it were, in some kind of relaxation, those who would like Canada to bleed herself white sometimes raise a clamour against " political patronage." As far as I am concerned, and I am sure many hon. members agree with me, I may say that I am now far from being spoilt as regards the " patronage " I can dispense to my electors. In support of that statement, I wish to quote a few paragraphs from a letter written to us on October 3, 1939, by the late lamented Minister of National Defence, the hon. Norman McLeod Rogers. The second paragraph reads as follows:
If Canada is to contribute her effort most effectively, it is absolutely necessary that _we all move forward in a complete unity of spirit and purpose. Partisan or personal preferences can have no place in our plans for prosecuting the war.
The letter then goes on:
This means that political interference or personal influence can have no effect in the appointment to commissions in various arms of the service, promotions and employment of civilian help by this department. It means also that purchases of wartime supplies will be made by the war supply board in the open market in the interest of economy and efficiency. No special consideration can be claimed by any particular firm. It is specifically requested that no favours be asked for with respect to contracts, appointments or employment. To grant such requests on a political or personal basis would impair the national character of our wartime effort.
A second letter was written to us by the three ministers of national defence on August 8, 1940. It said about the same things, but dealt with a much greater number of details. In addition to stating that preference should go to war veterans, a statement with which everyone agrees, that letter contained a paragraph which some officials have taken quite seriously:
It is the duty of the employing officer to select his help from those sent to him through any of the employment agencies mentioned above on the basis of qualifications to do the work. He shall not allow personal letters of recommendation (other than those written by former employers) on behalf of any applicant to influence him in this selection.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that some officials quote that paragraph with an eagerness and a patience that would be most creditable, were those people showing more judgment.
I took the liberty of replying to that letter as follows:
Dear Sir:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter dated August 8th, which is no doubt written for the particular information of members.
I am willing to comply with your request as regards appointments, promotions, transfers, and so on dn Canada's armed forces. I do not wish any action of mine to interfere with Canada's tremendous war effort.
Parliament has decided upon that war effort and, while not agreeing fully with its views, I must bow to the will of the majority.
However, I am the elected representative of the people of my constituency, and I cannot refuse to give a letter of recommendation to any elector who wishes to secure work on the various projects carried on in many places by the Department of National Defence, especially when I know that the man needs work. Those whom I recommend are honest and law abiding. I do not think any one of them guilty of any offence under the acts that have been passed.
_ In my district, most of the work is done in towns and in their close vicinity. I glean for my electors what little work is available for them. I cannot leave them under the impression that I am no longer able to deal with their requests, even in war time.
My letter goes on:
The opponents of the present government protest against political patronage, as they have indeed always done, so as to screen their activities in the various departments of the federal service. My point is sufficiently illustrated by what happens all too frequently in the civil service commission.
It is true that we are at war, but sooner or later peace will come. We shall then he in a position to determine whether our nation's effort has put too heavy a strain on our resources. We shall also be able to see whether priority has always been given to our Canadian fellow-citizens in those services. When the proper time comes, we can easily ascertain the situation and determine the extent of our war effort.
You may rest assured that my remarks are not promoted by the wish to voice any criticism. What makes me uneasy about the future is the fact that I foresee the very serious problems that will confront Canada after the war. I hope you will consider my statement not as a criticism but as a recital of facts.
Yours very truly,
I have had the privilege of an acknowledgment from the Minister of National Defence for Air.
I have therefore continued to give letters of recommendation without any qualms whatever, for, after all, my electors pay taxes like others, they serve just the same as others do. Some of them are even on active service overseas. Whenever they have the chance of earning some extra money and they believe that I can help them to secure employment, I do not wish to disappoint my constituents, and, whatever their political creed may be, I do my utmost, on all occasions, to secure work for them.
The Address-Mr. Gauthier

Before 1931, the great Valeartier camp was in the constituency of Portneuf, but a redistribution having been made, although that camp was normally a part of the county of Portneuf, by a mere pencil stroke it was detached from it and added to the constituency of Quebec-Montmorency. That is the only war industry in which the people from adjacent parishes may obtain occasional employment. I know that letters of recommendation have been ridiculed and even torn up by some officials. I only ask that this be not done in my presence. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that more judgment will be shown in future. I may add that all too often-I have ascertained the fact during the last few days- some kind of secret patronage system is set up among friends and that some of its most faithful devotees are outspoken supporters of the Conservative party. As I have rightly said, their purpose in raising a clamour is to screen their activities.
Some one was pointing out to me the other day that there was some danger for the people in rural areas if we insisted upon securing work for them in war industries. They might thus be attracted to town occupations and we might be unable to bring them back to the land. I have always held that agriculture is indispensable to us and that we should concentrate all our efforts upon making it successful so that it may become the life work of a larger number of people. But there are also, in my constituency, people who look for work because they need it. Paper factories, which had lately been working at their full capacity seem to curtail their production for the time being, and some people who were working a short time ago are now unemployed. They deserve all my support and I hope that employers in war industries will show them some consideration. I had much pleasure in listening to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Bellechasse, especially when he stated that the province of Quebec had not been given her full share of war contracts. I can tell you that my constituency has not been spoiled in that regard.
Huge plants are now being erected. There are in our province some factories of lesser importance which would certainly have proved useful in the production of many kinds of war supplies. I have taken the liberty of bringing them to the attention of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and I am now awaiting the result of that action.
A distinguished British statesman has recently said: "We have had the audacity to industrialize Canada." I fully agree with him. I do believe that if Europe is now plunged into a war brought about by economic difficul-

ties, it is to a great extent due to the fact that those continents which formerly imported industrial goods from Europe are today so organized as to be able to compete successfully with countries on the other side of the Atlantic. Since the improvement of machinery has enabled workmen to produce with the same amount of labour ten times more than the farmers, it is unavoidable that manufactured goods should glut the market more rapidly, and whereas trading could formerly be successfully carried on with agricultural nations it has now become ruinous on account of the industrialization of the latter. We are facing a similar threat.
Consequently, we will necessarily be compelled-and now is the time to do some planning in that regard-to concentrate our efforts upon a national programme of land settlement and a back-to-the-land movement. All Canadian provinces have for a long time carried on land settlement, but unfortunately they all too often lacked a definite programme. In a vast country like ours, while we should not rely too much on immigration, which is always dangerous, there is room for millions of people whom we should, more than ever, settle on the land. The opening of new rural communities always ensures new opportunities to skilled workmen and even to professional men. I have read somewhere about a settlement plan prepared by the head of the unemployment relief service in the provincial government of Quebec.
Time will not permit me to describe fully that plan, but I may say that it rightly provides first for such things as the opening of roads by the unemployed, the clearing of land, and its subdivision into lots, the building of houses, and it has two ends in view: lessening of unemployment and placing settlers permanently on the land.
I have taken the trouble to find out in the reports of the different federal and provincial departments the cost of unemployment relief work and direct relief from 1931 to 1940. I have found-my figures may not be quite accurate, but they are not far out- that, for the period mentioned, the province of Quebec alone has paid in relief about $49,000,000. The dominion's share is somewhat more than $44,000,000 and the municipalities have paid nearly $36,500,000. The expenditures have thus reached a total of nearly $130,000,000.
It is quite interesting to note the difference between the amounts spent on unemployment relief and the sums devoted to land settlement, including the back-to-the-land movement. For land settlement, the province and

The Address-Mr. Gauthier
the dominion have jointly spent about $8,000,000, the dominion's share being about $800,000 and the province's over $7,000,000. Thus, land settlement and the back-to-the-land movement have together cost $120,000,000 less than unemployment relief. And such a thing happened in a country considered as the richest in the world. If we add the sum of about $80,000,000 spent in the same province on relief work, we have a grand total of more than $220,000,000.
I may have seemed to digress in dealing with relief work and settlement, but my purpose was to give an inkling of the situation and to point out a phase of the problem with which we will be confronted when our war industries cease to operate, partly at least, for some of them will remain in existence, since war has become a permanent industry.
In those plants that will have to be closed, instead of making guns, tanks and machine guns, we shall have to build tractors, trucks and giant plows for tilling the Canadian soil, making it produce to its full capacity and continuing to give to our people the impression, which visitors from foreign lands sometimes gather, that after all Canada is God's own country.
Something has been said in this house about the fixing of prices for butter and other farm products. A farmer gave me, from memory, some prices that were prevailing during last war, from 1914 to 1918. To my mind, they show the great difference between the government of that time and the one we have to-day. That farmer told me that during the last war the wholesale price of butter was 75 cents and even more. That is more than twice the present price. And, if I remember well, prices had not been fixed. In 1917, the wholesale price of pork was 25 cents; to-day it is 10 or 11 cents. It has never entered the minds of our farmers to be war profiteers; they are doing nobly and courageously their share in the general effort. But before any fixing of prices, some notice will have to be taken of the prices they pay as consumers, for they are indeed the most important consumers and they are those who have had most to suffer during the last few years.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) on his splendid speech. He has asked that the salary of grade 1 clerks who are under the civil service commission be raised. I agree with him and I hope that his plea will receive the attention it deserves.
During the visit of our sovereigns, the king and queen of Canada, who are now giving to the world an example of courage that must astonish and confound the enemies of the
empire, I said that our sovereigns, after their passage in our midst, would have the recollection of a flagless country. There are perhaps many who do not believe as strongly as I do in the need of a national flag. It seems that the present time, when we are endeavouring to unite closely all the energies, activities, hopes and the aspirations of the Canadian nation, is perfectly suitable for the carrying out of the plan which has so often been discussed in this house and which would have deserved a better fate. Every country in the world has its flag, even our sister nations of the British commonwealth. Why should Canada have none? We venerate and respect the Union Jack, but it does not symbolize all that makes up the history of our country. We would gladly see it reproduced on a flag alongside the fleur-de-lis and the maple leaf. What stands in the way of the adopting of a national emblem in Canada? I am quite convinced that all Canadians would hail the presence of their flag of the design that was placed on the flag of the first Canadian contingent during the present war. Parliament and the government should not postpone such a necessary and ineluctable task until a movement arises, sooner or later, within the nation. If there are any who believe that the possession of a distinct flag is an unimportant matter for a country, let them take the trouble to observe what happens elsewhere. Does not the Union Jack call forth the admiration of Englishmen? Are the Americans unmoved by the star spangled banner? Why should the sight of our national flag leave us unconcerned? I believe that the citizens of a nation are stirred by the sight of their national flag as much as by the hearing of their national anthem. I should like all Canadians to raise their voices in demanding the immediate fulfilment of that project, and expressing afterwards their gratitude to those responsible for having given to their fatherland a truly national emblem.
(Text) In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it is a greait pleasure to me to commend the mover (Mr. Claxton) and the seconder (Mr. Jutras) of the address. They had a difficult task to perform, but they mastered it so well that every member of this house, irrespective of his political allegiance, must have found their performance more than satisfactory.
We have been told so many useful and promising things about national unity for many years, and particularly during the last few weeks, that it might seem useless to elaborate upon it. It seems a well established fact. Our unity must not be a make-believe, or smouldering embers only. My belief is

The Address-Mr. Gauthier

that to achieve real unity, the first essential is that every man living in this country must think of himself as a Canadian 'living here not in a temporary but a permanent homeland. Our point of view must be, above all, Canadian.
In this war effort some of us say that Canada must do everything, go to the utmost limit of our resources and man-power. We are at war, and we do not know how far it may lead us. Canada's possibilities and the industrial aid she can give to Britain are great owing to the large number of men we can count on to provide her with all the ammunition she will need.
Prominent British leaders call upon the United States and Canada for more aid. Before the defeat of France, Reynaud and Weygand were imploring for more material- not for men, but for material. Britain is also asking for more material. A satisfactory difference exists between this war and the last war. As far as Canada is concerned, the money is spent in Canada in a much larger proportion. This is a real Canadian action.
To fight for Christianity and democratic liberties is all very well, but we must see that after the war Canada has the strength to assure the survival of our democratic liberties, and keep this Canadian spirit of welfare and prosperity.
Then we will need that national unity, unity built up by unceasing efforts to observe and care for the details as well as for the important things. This country of ours has been built upon the basis of self-sacrifice, devotion, and respect of everyone's rights and privileges. That is the only way to build it up. We must go on in the same spirit.
A few minutes ago, I said that we should care for even the details. In many instances important matters have been forgotten. We know that our unceasing efforts to keep the free and official use of our French language must have wearied the protagonists of the "one language, one school" policy, but we know too, and everyone must realize, that this affection and attachment for our language, our religion, our traditions, made us feel that there was no land in the world, no country, no government as good and as just as Canada's, and our affection for and adhesion to these privileges and rights grew broader and went beyond the boundaries of the province, became nation-wide and Canadian through and through. This was the result of our tenacity.
We kept our mother tongue, religion, institutions and traditions. We fought for that and would fight to the end for these same

rights; and this tenacity we still possess and make use of for the prosperity and defence of our Canada.
Speaking in French I asked the government and the house to give Canada a national flag. Our history, our aspirations, the present circumstances call for a national flag. Canada has been existing, living, growing for four centuries; still she cannot look with pride to her own national emblem. I believe we have waited long enough. A certain class of Canadians may think this a detail, but it must have some meaning since every nation has a flag of its own.
I should like to hear everyone in this country calling for and urging the government and parliament to give our country the flag we need. A national anthem, a national flag, a completed autonomy, a perfect national unity, and Canada will be a real nation.
